items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that for a quadratic equation

Content:
[MATH: ax^2 + bx + c = 0,]
with [MATH: a\neq 0,] the discriminant is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{D} = b^2 - 4ac.]

Content:
A quadratic equation has no real solutions if the discriminant is negative: [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0.]

Content:
If a quadratic equation contains an unknown parameter and we know the equation has no real solutions, we can use the condition [MATH: \mathcal D < 0] to place conditions on the unknown parameter.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's consider the equation

Content:
[MATH: 2x^2-5kx+10 = 0]
where [MATH: k] is a real parameter. We wish to find all the values of [MATH: k] for which the quadratic equation has no real solutions.

Content:
To compute the discriminant, we first note that the coefficients are
[MATH: a=2,\quad b=-5k,\quad c=10.]

Content:
So, we require

Content:
[MATH: D|< 0; b^{2} − 4ac|< 0; (− 5k)^{2} − 4(2)(10)|< 0; 25k^{2} − 80|< 0]

Content:
This is a quadratic inequality in the variable [MATH: k.] Solving this equation for [MATH: k,] we get the following:
[MATH: 25k^{2} − 80|< 0; 25k^{2}|< 80; k^{2}|< (16)/(5); sqrt(k^{2})|< sqrt((16)/(5));|k||< (4)/(sqrt(5));|k||< (4sqrt(5))/(5).]

Content:
Therefore, our solution is
[MATH: -\dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{5} < k < \dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{5}.]

Content:
We can also express this solution using interval notation:

Content:
[MATH: k \in \left(-\dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{5},\dfrac{4\sqrt{5}}{5}\right)]

Content:
Any value of [MATH: k] in this interval will give a quadratic equation with no real solutions.

So, we require

[MATH: D|< 0; b^{2} − 4ac|< 0; (6)^{2} − 4(k)(k)|< 0; 36 − 4k^{2}|< 0; 36|< 4k^{2}; k^{2}|> 9; sqrt(k^{2})|> sqrt(9);|k||> 3.]

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: x(px - 24) = -9,] where [MATH: p] is an integer constant, has no real solutions, what is the least possible value of [MATH: p?]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: x(px - 24) = -9,] where [MATH: p] is an integer constant, has no real solutions, what is the least possible value of [MATH: p?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A quadratic equation has no real solutions if the discriminant is negative: [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0.]

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

[MATH: x(px − 24)|= − 9; px^{2} − 24x|= − 9; px^{2} − 24x + 9|= 0]

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = p, \qquad b = -24, \qquad c = 9]

So, computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = (− 24)^{2} − 4(p)(9); = 576 − 36p.]

To have no real solutions, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0{:}]

[MATH: 576 − 36p|< 0; − 36p|< − 576; p|> (− 576)/(− 36); p|> 16]

Since [MATH: p] must be an integer, we conclude that the least possible value is [MATH: 17.]
